verified.title: Transformers Learn In-Context by Gradient Descent
verified.authors: Johannes von Oswald, Eyvind Niklasson, Ettore Randazzo, Joao Sacramento, Alexander Mordvintsev, Andrey Zhmoginov, Max Vladymyrov
verified.key_finding: Proposition 1 constructs a single linear self-attention layer whose output equals one GD step on the squared regression loss L(W) = (1/2N) sum_i ||W x_i - y_i||^2, giving dW = -(eta/N) sum_i (W x_i - y_i) x_i^T. Both factors are absorbed into the projection (P = (eta/N) I), and the learning rate 'can be implicitly (meta-)learned'. K stacked layers give about K steps. Trained deeper models beat plain GD, and the authors describe them as GD++, an iterative curvature correction using H(X) = I - gamma X X^T. The main experiments use attention-only models trained from scratch on (x, y) regression tokens. Softmax attention plus LayerNorm still learns this way but performs 'worse than when using linear self-attention' (judged 'suboptimal'). Nonlinear tasks need MLPs placed before attention. With alternating x/y tokens, a softmax first layer is needed to copy the tokens. The link to LLMs is stated as Hypothesis 1.
verified.relation: This explains our result as a matter of magnitude; it does not contradict it. In the construction, one layer gives one averaged step whose effective lr (eta/N) is fixed by the weights. It follows (this is our inference; the paper does not say it) that a pretrained model gives no automatic reason for 16 in-context rows to match the cumulative effect of 76 Adam steps at lr 5e-4. The theory is only shown for toy regression models, so it is motivation, not evidence about Qwen3.
verified.verification_note: Venue confirmed on PMLR (v202/von-oswald23a). Formula, P = (eta/N)I, GD++, and Hypothesis 1 confirmed in the text. Corrected the softmax wording: the original said softmax 'needed extra mechanisms'. In fact softmax/LayerNorm performed worse with no number given, MLPs were added for nonlinear tasks, and softmax was needed for copying. The paper never states that 'more demos do not make the update bigger'; that is our reading of the 1/N factor.

verified.title: Why Can GPT Learn In-Context? Language Models Secretly Perform Gradient Descent as Meta-Optimizers
verified.authors: Damai Dai, Yutao Sun, Li Dong, Yaru Hao, Shuming Ma, Zhifang Sui, Furu Wei
verified.venue: Findings of ACL 2023, pp. 4005-4019 (arXiv:2212.10559, titled '...Implicitly Perform...')
verified.key_finding: With softmax and scaling dropped (relaxed linear attention), attention to the demo tokens becomes an additive update dW_ICL = sum_i (W_V x'_i)(W_K x'_i)^T on top of W_ZSL. The fine-tuning baseline updates only the K/V projections with SGD, one step per demonstration, in demo order, for one epoch. Its lr is chosen from a 36-value grid by validation performance. Models were fairseq GPT 1.3B and 2.7B on six classification datasets (SST2, SST5, MR, Subj, AGNews, CB). ICL recovers more than 85% of the examples that FT corrects (Rec2FTP averages 85.56 and 89.39). SimAOU(dFT) averages 0.186 for 1.3B (range 0.080-0.281) and 0.225 for 2.7B (range 0.130-0.333). Random updates score about 0.002 and -0.001.
verified.relation: Under this most generous published equivalence, 16 in-context rows are at best like one K/V-only SGD pass over 16 examples, and it is judged by label accuracy on in-distribution classification. Our FT is far outside that regime: about 300 example-gradients, LoRA, Adam, and an off-task generation-format metric. On a budget-matched reading (about 4 rows per step, so 16 rows is about step 4), FT already moves the format by step 8 while ICL stays near zero. This suggests ICL is weaker than budget-matched GD here. That is our inference; Dai et al. did not test it.
verified.verification_note: The arXiv PDF was not machine-readable, so the full text was read on ar5iv. Title corrected to the Findings of ACL version ('Secretly Perform'); arXiv and the ICLR workshop version use 'Implicitly Perform'. The SimAOU range was widened to 0.08-0.33 because the original covered only the 1.3B model. Added that the optimizer is SGD. All other details were confirmed.

verified.title: Learning without training: The implicit dynamics of in-context learning
verified.authors: Benoit Dherin, Michael Munn, Hanna Mazzawi, Michael Wunder, Javier Gonzalvo
verified.venue: arXiv preprint 2507.16003 (Google Research; v4 June 2026, no venue or journal-ref listed)
verified.key_finding: For a contextual block (a contextual layer such as attention, followed by an MLP), the output with context equals the output without context after a rank-1 update of the first MLP weight matrix: dW_x(Y) = (W dA_x(Y)) A(C\Y, x)^T / ||A(C\Y, x)||^2. For Y = C this reduces to (W dA_x(C)) A(x)^T / ||A(x)||^2. The authors say the update is 'dynamic and depend[s] on the input query tokens'. Feeding tokens one at a time gives SGD-like updates with lr 1/||A(x)||^2, and the increments shrink and vanish. Agreement was about 1e-7 for one layer and about 1e-6 for 10 stacked blocks with LayerNorm. All experiments use synthetic linear regression (d=2, N=100); no pretrained LLM is evaluated.
verified.relation: This is the most direct mechanistic handle on our split, but it is a hypothesis for our setting. The implicit update is recomputed per query and scales with dA_x(C), the change that context causes in that query's attention output. If GSM8K tokens barely attend to the advice turns, the implicit update for math queries is near zero. LoRA, by contrast, is one static dW applied to every input. That fits the missing cross-domain transfer and the partial in-domain shortening (396 to 215 words). Neither the paper nor we have measured dA_x on real LLMs yet; it can be checked directly in Qwen3.
verified.verification_note: Confirmed in v3: formula, query dependence, lr 1/||A(x)||^2, vanishing increments, 1e-7 and 1e-6 figures, no pretrained LLM. The abs page shows a v4 (2 Jun 2026) with no venue. In v4 the theorem is renumbered 2.3 and framed as a 'minimal token-patch', the reported precision is 10^-6, and the experiments are still linear regression only (one uses a pretrained toy transformer).

verified.title: Position: Do pretrained Transformers Learn In-Context by Gradient Descent?
verified.authors: Lingfeng Shen, Aayush Mishra, Daniel Khashabi
verified.key_finding: The authors argue that ICL=GD constructions rest on assumptions far from real LM training: models trained on the ICL objective, hand-built sparse weights (real LLaMA is much less sparse), and linear attention. They test LLaMA-7B on AGNews, CB, SST-2 and RTE with 1, 2, 4 and 8 demos. GD fine-tunes on the same demos for 200 epochs with lr in {1e-4, 5e-4, 1e-5, 5e-5}. GD^ variants update only W_V of one middle or one deep layer. On all three metrics there is 'a clear gap' between ICL and every GD variant: full-vocabulary accuracy, top-10 token overlap, and overlap cosine similarity. ICL compared with reordered ICL overlaps more than ICL compared with GD. Apart from early-epoch checkpoints, most pairs of GD checkpoints have small token overlap and OCS ('how drastically GD based learning changes the model's behavior'). ICL is more order-sensitive than GD, SGD or Adam.
verified.relation: This is evidence that in a real pretrained LM the two routes give different output distributions, not scaled versions of the same one. That fits the per-dataset Spearman of -0.08 between ICL and FT effects. The paper shows that GD reshapes outputs drastically. It does not claim that ICL acts 'locally'; that part of the analogy to our FT-everywhere vs ICL-barely pattern is our own reading.
verified.verification_note: Venue confirmed via PMLR v235/shen24d and the ICML virtual site. The proceedings title starts with 'Position:'. Corrections: the lr grid is {1e-4, 5e-4, 1e-5, 5e-5}, not '1e-4 to 5e-5'. The text says 'fine-tune the models' and does not explicitly say full-model. 'GD checkpoints diverge quickly' was reworded to what the paper reports: apart from early epochs, checkpoint pairs show low overlap.

verified.title: In-context Learning and Gradient Descent Revisited
verified.authors: Gilad Deutch, Nadav Magar, Tomer Bar Natan, Guy Dar
verified.key_finding: Re-running Dai et al.'s metrics, untrained models get 'comparable' ICL-GD similarity (abstract); the body says 'at least as good as trained ones'. Their SimAOU slightly exceeds vanilla GD on most tasks, e.g. SST2 0.09 vs 0.05 (CB is an exception: 0.04 vs 0.11). SimAM_delta is mixed: untrained vs trained is 0.11/0.05/0.16/0.17/0.26 vs 0.15/0.31/0.14/0.25/0.25 on SST2/SST5/MR/Subj/CB. The paper names a mismatch 'layer causality': in ICL a layer's hidden state depends only on shallower layers, while GD gradients reach every layer, including from deeper ones. Layer-causal GD raises average SimAOU from 0.102 to 0.167. SimAM_delta deliberately ignores update magnitude, since update size 'can be manipulated by adjusting the learning rate'.
verified.relation: The published 'ICL behaves like FT' evidence is near an untrained-model baseline, so there was no strong prior that the per-dataset ICL effect would track the FT effect (it does not: -0.08). The standard similarity metrics are built to ignore magnitude, so they cannot speak to the magnitude gap our result shows. Layer causality suggests a mechanism: FT can push the terse-verdict loss back into early layers and change how any prompt is processed, while context only adds keys and values that later queries may or may not read. This is our hypothesis.
verified.verification_note: Venue confirmed on the ACL Anthology (2024.naacl-long.58). The arXiv author is 'Tomer Bar Natan'; the Anthology lists 'Tomer Natan'. Corrected 'at least as high' (true for SimAOU on most tasks but not uniformly; SimAM_delta is mixed). Added SST5, where trained is 0.31 vs untrained 0.05, which the original omitted. The relation's 'no one has measured magnitude' was softened to a statement about these metrics.

verified.title: In-context Vectors: Making In Context Learning More Effective and Controllable Through Latent Space Steering
verified.authors: Sheng Liu, Haotian Ye, Lei Xing, James Zou
verified.key_finding: The authors treat ICL as a shift of latent states where 'the direction of the shift and the distance of the shift are automatically controlled by the self-attention mechanism'. The ICV is the first principal direction of the last-token latent differences h(y_i) - h(x_i), concatenated over layers. It is added at all layers and token positions with lambda = 0.1 by default, and the result is rescaled to keep the original norm. Llama-7b formality: no context 17.54, ICL 32.96, LoRA FT 21.99, ICV 48.30. Falcon-7b ParaDetox toxicity (lower is better): ICL 73.09, LoRA 52.78, ICV 34.77. Vicuna-7b jailbreak ASR: ICL 44, ICV 50 at lambda 0.10, 93 at 0.18, 99 at 0.20. Single-layer ICV gives toxicity 76-79% against 79.84 with no ICV and 34.77 at all layers.
verified.relation: This supports a 'right direction, too little magnitude or gating' reading for style-type behaviour. Demos encode a usable style direction, which plain ICL applies only weakly through attention, and the effect grows with lambda. A direct test for us: extract an ICV from the 16 advice rows, add it to all tokens (query-independent, like LoRA), and sweep lambda. If math working drops, the gap is magnitude and query-gating. If not, the context route encodes a different direction from the one FT installs.
verified.verification_note: Venue confirmed on PMLR (v235/liu24bx). Removed the claim that 'plain ICL is the weakest option'. On formality, LoRA FT (21.99) scores below ICL (32.96); ICL is worst only on ParaDetox. Added that the jailbreak numbers are on Vicuna-7b, the norm rescaling, and the no-ICV baseline for the single-layer ablation.

verified.title: Emergent Misalignment via In-Context Learning: Narrow in-context examples can produce broadly misaligned LLMs
verified.authors: Nikita Afonin, Nikita Andriyanov, Vahagn Hovhannisyan, Nikhil Bageshpura, Kyle Liu, Kevin Zhu, Sunishchal Dev, Ashwinee Panda, Oleg Rogov, Elena Tutubalina, Alexander Panchenko, Mikhail Seleznyov
verified.key_finding: The authors test 11 frontier models: Gemini 2.5 Pro/Flash and 3 Pro/Flash, Kimi-K2 0905 and Thinking, Grok 4 and 4.1 Fast, Qwen3-Max, and Qwen3-Next-80B Instruct and Thinking. With 16 narrow examples in 'Prompt:/Response:' format, all in the first user message, emergent misalignment on unrelated questions is about 1-24%. It appears with as few as 2 examples (Gemini 3 Pro) and generally rises from 2 to 32 examples. Incorrect but non-harmful TruthfulQA examples produced EM in 8 of 9 models; Qwen3-Next-80B Instruct showed none. Insecure-code examples produced no EM in any model, which the authors attribute to a format mismatch (Betley et al. also found none in GPT-4o with up to 256 examples). Scale showed no reliable correlation with EM. Proposed mechanism: a conflict between safety and context-following. Telling the model to prioritise context-following raises EM; prioritising safety lowers it.
verified.relation: This is a counterpoint. The context route can install broad off-domain side effects, even from incorrect but non-harmful answers, which is close to our 'incorrect_answer' data. But here that happens in frontier models, with demos in one prompt, for a disposition-type trait. Our null comes from a 1.7B chat model, demos as earlier user/assistant turns, and a format trait. That leaves open whether our gap comes from the route, model capacity, or how the demos are presented. Their insecure-code null shows that context transfer depends on demo format.
verified.verification_note: Acceptance confirmed: ACL Anthology lists it as 2026.acl-long.1770 (ACL 2026, pp. 38197-38212). Type changed from preprint to peer_reviewed and year to 2026. The full author list was added. Numbers differ across arXiv versions (v1: 2-17% with 64 examples); v3 and the final version report 1-24% with 16 examples. Added the TruthfulQA result and the scale non-correlation, both relevant to our setup.

verified.title: What In-Context Learning 'Learns' In-Context: Disentangling Task Recognition and Task Learning
verified.authors: Jane Pan, Tianyu Gao, Howard Chen, Danqi Chen
verified.key_finding: Across GPT-3, LLaMA and OPT on classification datasets, ICL splits into task recognition (TR) and task learning (TL). TR identifies the task and applies pretrained priors, and works with non-trivial performance even without correct labels. TL acquires new input-label mappings. TR 'does not further improve with larger models or more demonstrations'. 'LLMs acquire TL as the model scales', and TL 'consistently improves with more demonstrations in context'.
verified.relation: At 1.7B with 16 shots, the context is probably used mainly for recognition. On a GSM8K query the model recognises 'math' and falls back on its strong prior to show working, so the terse-verdict mapping is never learned as a rule that crosses tasks. This predicts that the in-context effect should grow with model size and shot count. It is our extrapolation, since the paper studies only in-task classification, not cross-task format transfer.
verified.verification_note: Only the arXiv abstract page was read, which lists 'Accepted to Findings of ACL 2023'. The abstract confirms the models, the TR/TL split, and both scaling statements. The full text was not read.

verified.title: On the generalization of language models from in-context learning and finetuning: a controlled study
verified.authors: Andrew K. Lampinen, Arslan Chaudhry, Stephanie C.Y. Chan, Cody Wild, Diane Wan, Alex Ku, Jorg Bornschein, Razvan Pascanu, Murray Shanahan, James L. McClelland
verified.key_finding: On Gemini 1.5 Flash (plus a Flash-8B comparison), the same data was given either in context or via FT (batch 8-16, lr 3e-4, 200-1000 steps). ICL generalized better to reversals and syllogisms. On the reversal-curse set, FT is near zero on reversals while full-dataset ICL is near ceiling. Adding in-context inferences to the FT data improves FT and on several splits matches or beats ICL. The authors attribute the gap to differing inductive biases, citing rule- vs exemplar-based generalization and a simplicity bias for ICL. They added QA examples so FT would not degrade QA, but did not measure off-task side effects or behavioural drift.
verified.relation: This complements our result. The two routes generalize along different axes: ICL generalizes better to content inferences from given facts, while our data show FT spreads an incidental surface format far more widely, into math. Both are hard to square with 'ICL is just a small fine-tune'. Their augmentation remedy suggests a test: fine-tune on the in-context model's own outputs (context distillation) and check whether the format side effect still appears.
verified.verification_note: The arXiv abs comments say 'FoRLM workshop, NeurIPS 2025'; I kept the type as preprint because it is a workshop paper. The author list matches the abs page. Hyperparameters, reversal and syllogism results, augmentation, and the inductive-bias explanation were all confirmed.

open_questions: Is the context effect just too small, or pointed in the wrong direction? We could build an in-context vector or task vector from the 16 rows and inject it into every token at increasing scale lambda (Liu et al. 2024), then check whether GSM8K working drops. Separately, we could compare the residual-stream shift that FT causes on GSM8K prompts with the shift the context causes, using a cosine metric checked against an untrained or random baseline as Deutch et al. recommend.

Do the GSM8K queries actually read from the advice context? Following Dherin et al., the implicit update for a query scales with its context vector dA_x(C) = A(C,x) - A(x). Measuring ||dA_x(C)|| per layer for advice queries and for math queries would test whether the implicit 'fine-tune' for math is close to zero. If so, the context route behaves like a gated, query-local update, while LoRA is one static update applied everywhere.

What happens with a budget-matched, Dai-style 'ICL-equivalent' fine-tune: the same 16 rows, one step per row, one epoch, K/V-only or attention-only LoRA, learning rate tuned? If it also fails to install the format, the gap is about regime (about 300 example-gradients, Adam, MLP/LoRA capacity, 2 epochs) rather than about route. If it does install the format, then ICL is weaker than even matched GD. Given that FT reaches half its effect by step 8 (about 32 rows, assuming about 4 rows per step), the second outcome looks likely.

Do scale, shot count and presentation turn the context route on? The in-context effect could be measured with many-shot context (64-256 rows), with all demos in a single prompt instead of earlier chat turns (the Afonin et al. setup), and on Qwen3-14B instead of 1.7B. Pan et al.'s task-learning-emerges-with-scale result predicts growth. It is also worth checking whether a larger in-context effect would then start to correlate with the FT effect per dataset.

How much of the FT format spillover depends on gradients flowing back from the output loss into early layers, which ICL cannot do (Deutch et al.'s 'layer causality')? LoRA could be restricted to late layers versus early layers, or trained with a layer-causal objective, to see whether off-domain format transfer shrinks. A related check: is the near-zero per-dataset in-context effect reliable enough (split-half) for a Spearman correlation to mean anything at all?

verified.title: Larger language models do in-context learning differently
verified.authors: Jerry Wei, Jason Wei, Yi Tay, Dustin Tran, Albert Webson, Yifeng Lu, Xinyun Chen, Hanxiao Liu, Da Huang, Denny Zhou, Tengyu Ma
verified.key_finding: With flipped labels, small models' accuracy 'remains relatively flat and often does not dip below random guessing, even when 100% of labels are flipped', so they do not override semantic priors. Large models follow the flipped demos (text-davinci-002 drops from 90.3% at 0% flipped to 22.5% at 100% flipped). Instruction tuning strengthens both the use of semantic priors and the learning of input-label mappings, but more of the former: Flan-PaLM could not override its semantics beyond what random guessing achieves even at 100% flipped labels, while plain PaLM went as low as 31%.
verified.relation: Explains our result, by analogy. Qwen3-1.7B-chat is small and heavily post-trained, the regime where demonstrations that cut against a strong default get discounted. Caveat: the paper tests flipped or unrelated labels on the same classification task with base and Flan models. Our case is a different task (advice demos, math query), so carrying this over to an answer-format prior is our inference. Fine-tuning edits the prior directly and is not limited this way.
verified.verification_note: Title, authors and the 90.3% -> 22.5%, Flan-PaLM and 31% figures checked verbatim in the arXiv HTML. The arXiv page has no comments or journal-ref field, and a search found no accepted conference version. Small models here are GPT-3 ada/babbage, PaLM-8B and similar. URL changed to the abs page; the HTML version is identical.

verified.title: Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations: What Makes In-Context Learning Work?
verified.authors: Sewon Min, Xinxi Lyu, Ari Holtzman, Mikel Artetxe, Mike Lewis, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Luke Zettlemoyer
verified.key_finding: Replacing gold labels with random labels costs only 0-5% absolute (1.7% on average for multi-choice, 2.6% for classification). With Direct MetaICL, random corpus sentences randomly paired with the label set, in the right format, keep 95% (classification) and 82% (multi-choice) of the ICL gain. Swapping demo inputs for out-of-distribution corpus text cuts performance by 3-16% absolute for Channel MetaICL and Direct/Channel GPT-J (Direct MetaICL is the exception). The authors hypothesise that meta-training makes models 'almost exclusively exploit simpler aspects of the demonstrations like the format'.
verified.relation: Partly explains our result. Demonstrations act mainly through format, label space and input distribution, and they help less when their inputs do not match the test distribution. That fits our pattern: in context, advice answers shrink (396 -> 215 words) while GSM8K working stays at 0.99. Caveat: Min et al. always test on the demos' own task. They never test whether a demo format carries over to a different task such as a math query, so 'the format is conditioned on advice-type input' is our extrapolation. Fine-tuning has no such conditioning and spreads the format globally.
verified.verification_note: All numbers checked verbatim in the ar5iv text (Sections 4.1, 5.1, 5.3, 5.4). Corrected: the 95% figure is for classification only (82% for multi-choice), and the OOD drop applies to three of the four model variants, not all.

verified.title: What In-Context Learning 'Learns' In-Context: Disentangling Task Recognition and Task Learning
verified.authors: Jane Pan, Tianyu Gao, Howard Chen, Danqi Chen
verified.key_finding: Task recognition (TR: identifying the task from demos and applying pretrained priors) already works in small models. With 8 examples, the 350M models lead the random baseline by around 10 points (GPT-3 ada) and 5 points (OPT-350M), and TR 'does not drastically scale with model sizes or numbers of examples'. Task learning (TL: picking up new label mappings) emerges only at scale: with 16 examples, OPT-66B and davinci (175B) match Gold performance under a new label mapping, while smaller models stay roughly flat as demos are added.
verified.relation: Explains our result, with caveats. For a 1.7B model, demonstrations mainly drive task recognition. A GSM8K query is recognised as math and the math prior (working) applies. Learning a new rule like 'always answer tersely' from 16 turns would be task learning, which small models barely do. This frames the in-context effect as a different mechanism rather than a weaker version of the fine-tuning effect, consistent with the uncorrelated per-dataset effects (Spearman -0.08). Caveat: the paper uses base models (GPT-3, OPT, LLaMA-1) on classification label mappings, not chat models or answer formats, so the transfer to our setting is inferred.
verified.verification_note: Findings checked verbatim in the ar5iv text. The venue was confirmed through the ACL Anthology entry 2023.findings-acl.527, and the URL was changed to that entry. The arXiv/ar5iv version (2305.09731) has the same content.

verified.title: Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Prompting: Zero-shot Can Be Stronger than Few-shot
verified.authors: Xiang Cheng, Chengyan Pan, Minjun Zhao, Deyang Li, Fangchao Liu, Xinyu Zhang, Xiao Zhang, Yong Liu
verified.key_finding: For recent instruction-tuned models (Qwen2.5 0.5B-72B, LLaMA3, Gemma2) on GSM8K/MATH, CoT exemplars do not improve reasoning over zero-shot CoT once answer-extraction bias is corrected (Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct GSM8K: 8-shot 95.75 vs zero-shot-fix 95.83; uncorrected zero-shot 91.58). 'The primary function of CoT exemplars is to align the output format.' On Qwen2.5-7B, attention shows the model 'largely ignores exemplars during inference, relying more on the prompt template.' Zero-shot was best for LLaMA3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-1.5B, but weaker or older models (LLaMA3.2-1B, LLaMA2-7B, Qwen-7B) gain significantly from exemplars. The 'base models rely more on exemplars' claim rests on a single Qwen2.5-72B base result.
verified.relation: Mixed. It supports the view that in-context exemplars barely change how capable instruction-tuned Qwen models reason on math. It contradicts the idea that these models hold to their own math answer format against the context: in this paper, changing output format is exactly what in-domain exemplars do. So our null in-context effect is probably not because Qwen ignores format cues in context in general. More likely our demos are cross-domain (advice), which fits Min et al. The paper itself says model strength is not defined by the degree of instruction tuning and has only one base model, so it does not support 'post-training makes the model ignore the context'.
verified.verification_note: Author list completed from the arXiv abs page (Comments: EMNLP 2025 Findings camera-ready). Numbers and quotes checked verbatim in the v3 HTML. Key finding and relation were corrected: exemplars do shift format, weaker models benefit, and the base-vs-instruct evidence is a single model.

verified.title: Is In-Context Learning Sufficient for Instruction Following in LLMs?
verified.authors: Hao Zhao, Maksym Andriushchenko, Francesco Croce, Nicolas Flammarion
verified.key_finding: In-context alignment (URIAL) of base models trails the official instruct models (SFT+RLHF) on MT-Bench in most cases (e.g. Llama-3-8B average 5.75 vs 7.86). Even with high-quality demos it plateaus after 10-30 examples. On an already instruct-tuned model (Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2), URIAL lowered scores (1st turn 7.92 -> 7.58, 2nd turn 7.18 -> 6.48), even rules alone hurt, and more examples gave larger declines. In a matched-data comparison on base models, ICL and IFT are 'roughly equivalent for single-turn conversations in the low-data regime' (Llama-3.1-8B: ICL even better at 3-30 demos). For the 2nd turn the trends are nearly opposite: IFT improves with more data and generalizes beyond the single-turn training format, while ICL with single-turn demos degrades.
verified.relation: Supports our result, with a nuance. In-context examples move an instruct model little and can disrupt its default behaviour. The matched-data result is the closest parallel to our side effect: on the trained task, ICL and fine-tuning are similar at low data. Off-distribution (2nd turn), fine-tuning carries the learned behaviour over and ICL does not. Similarly, fine-tuning spreads the terse format to GSM8K while 16 in-context turns do not. The plateau suggests more rows may not close the gap.
verified.verification_note: Venue from the arXiv comments ('Accepted at ICLR 2025'); arXiv v1 dates from 2024. Table 1, Table 7 and the Section 4 quotes were checked verbatim. Corrected: the plateau is after 10-30 examples, not 20-30. The 'instruction fine-tuning' side of Table 1 is the official instruct models, not same-data fine-tuning. The single-turn-hurts-2nd-turn result is shown on the base Mistral-7B-v0.2. The matched-data ICL vs IFT result was added.

verified.title: Bayesian scaling laws for in-context learning
verified.authors: Aryaman Arora, Dan Jurafsky, Christopher Potts, Noah D. Goodman
verified.key_finding: ICL is modelled as a Bayesian learner whose task prior (rho), ICL efficiency (K) and per-example likelihoods (P) give a scaling law in the number of shots. In synthetic GPT-2/HMM experiments, 'smaller amounts of post-training strongly change the prior over tasks but not the model's knowledge of each task'. Under SFT the prior 'suddenly shifts', and the post-training needed to suppress ICL of disfavoured tasks grows with scale. ICL can re-elicit behaviours suppressed by SFT/DPO, and the law predicts when. For Llama-3.1-8B, instruction tuning 'does reduce the prior probability of unsafe behaviours' but 'fails to prevent many-shot jailbreaking'; the posterior eventually saturates.
verified.relation: Gives a mechanistic frame for the asymmetry. LoRA fine-tuning on 150 rows rewrites the prior over response formats directly; the 'sudden shift' of the prior under SFT fits reaching half the effect after 8 of 76 steps. 16 in-context rows are only likelihood evidence against a strong post-trained prior for working on math, so the posterior barely moves. A shot-count dose-response rather than zero effect is our own prediction from the law, not a result of the paper.
verified.verification_note: Venue from the arXiv comments (COLM 2025 camera-ready); arXiv v1 dates from Oct 2024. Quotes checked in the v3 HTML. verified.key_finding: With 16 narrow in-context examples, EM rates range from 1% to 24% across Gemini, Kimi-K2, Grok and Qwen, and EM appears with as few as 2 examples. verified.title: Self-Training Elicits Concise Reasoning in Large Language Models
verified.authors: Tergel Munkhbat, Namgyu Ho, Seo Hyun Kim, Yongjin Yang, Yujin Kim, Se-Young Yun
verified.key_finding: 8-shot concise GSM8K exemplars, given as chat user/assistant turns, shorten small models' working substantially. FS-Human cuts GSM8K tokens by about 36% on average (relative length 64.4%): Llama-3.2-3B -48%, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B -64% (305.9 -> 111.2), Qwen2.5-3B -22% (301.1 -> 233.8), Gemma-2-2B -22%. Effects vary by exemplar source (Qwen2.5-3B FS-GPT4o only -1.6%). The authors state that 'few-shot prompting reliably elicits concise generations across all models', beating best-of-256 sampling. A zero-shot 'be concise' instruction moves the math-specialised models by under 1% (Qwen2.5-3B: -14%). Self-training on few-shot-conditioned short samples gives 64-78% relative length (FS-Human 68.0%) at 97-100% relative accuracy, without exemplars at test time.
verified.relation: Contradicts the 'math working is sticky against context' reading and sharpens our explanation. With in-domain concise math demos in the same chat-turn format we use, the context route shortens small models' working about as much as fine-tuning does (FS-Human prompting 64.4% vs self-training 68.0% relative length). So the in-context channel can carry format in small chat models. Our null (working 1.00 -> 0.99) points to the cross-domain gap between advice demos and a math query. Fine-tuning's distinctive property is that the format persists zero-shot and off-domain.

verified.key_finding: Attack success grows with shot count as a power law, tested up to 256 shots, and 'entirely benign examples of in-context learning follow similar power laws'. Fine-tuning the model to refuse such attacks 'merely delayed the jailbreak' to higher shot counts.

That it predicts a larger in-context effect at 14B, and noisy per-dataset rankings at 16 shots (consistent with ICL failing to predict 14B transfer), is our inference, not tested in the source.

The NeurIPS 2024 main-track paper was confirmed via the mlanthology entry, whose abstract matches: a power law up to hundreds of shots. The full paper PDF was not read. Author list taken from mlanthology, with its typos 'Fracesco' and 'Lanhan' corrected.

open_questions: Is the context route weak or just slow? Measure a dose-response with 16/64/256 in-context rows (power law as in Anil/Arora, or a plateau as in Zhao et al.) and compare it with the fine-tuning curve per step.

Is the in-context format shift domain-gated (task recognition per Pan et al. / Min et al.)? Control: terse in-domain math demos (GSM8K question -> bare number) versus the advice demos. If math demos make math terse but advice demos do not, the asymmetry is cross-task generalisation rather than channel strength.

How much does chat/RL post-training explain the resistance? Run the same 16-row context on the Qwen3-1.7B base model and on Qwen3-14B-chat. Wei et al. and Cheng et al. predict base > chat and large > small in demo-following.

Does the model attend to the demo turns at all when answering math (an attention or ablation analysis as in Cheng et al.)? Does the placement matter (earlier assistant turns vs examples quoted in the user turn vs a system prompt with an explicit 'answer tersely')?

Does fine-tuning install a global format prior (Arora: SFT shifts the prior over tasks)? Check whether the fine-tuning effect is concentrated in the first answer tokens / stylistic tokens and holds regardless of domain, and whether a few in-context math demos with working can push it back.

verified.title: Few-shot Fine-tuning vs. In-context Learning: A Fair Comparison and Evaluation
verified.authors: Marius Mosbach, Tiago Pimentel, Shauli Ravfogel, Dietrich Klakow, Yanai Elazar
verified.key_finding: The study compares ICL and pattern-based FT (PBFT) on OPT models from 125M to 30B, using 16 examples for ICL and 16 or more for FT. Its headline is that the two approaches generalize similarly, with large variance. With 16 examples, FT matches ICL in-domain, and for the largest model (OPT-30B) FT beats ICL both in-domain and OOD and keeps improving with more data. OOD on MNLI and QQP, most ICL models sit near the majority baseline, and only OPT-30B generalizes well on MNLI, in 4 of 10 runs. Some FT runs 'change their generalization strategy' and undergo 'a dramatic change in OOD performance after 75 steps'.
verified.relation: Partly supports our result. ICL at small and medium scale stays close to baseline OOD, while FT can move OOD behavior. But the paper's own framing is that the two are similar, and its smallest FT models also generalized poorly OOD, so the claim that ICL barely moves behavior while FT moves it strongly at small scale should be softened. The abrupt mid-training strategy switches fit our fast saturation (half the effect after 8 of 76 steps). Caveat: the tasks are classification (NLI, paraphrase), not output format.
verified.verification_note: Read the full PDF via pdftotext. Title, authors and venue are confirmed. The 'after 75 steps' and '4 out of 10 runs' quotes are verbatim. I added that the abstract says 'both approaches generalize similarly', which tempers 'matched or beat'.

verified.title: On the generalization of language models from in-context learning and finetuning: a controlled study
verified.authors: Andrew K. Lampinen, Arslan Chaudhry, Stephanie C. Y. Chan, Cody Wild, Diane Wan, Alex Ku, Jörg Bornschein, Razvan Pascanu, Murray Shanahan, James L. McClelland
verified.venue: FoRLM Workshop at NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv 2505.00661, v3 Nov 2025)
verified.key_finding: On Gemini 1.5 Flash with matched data, ICL over the training documents performs near ceiling on reversals while plain FT is near zero. ICL and augmented FT both beat FT with t>149, p<1e-16. On the large datasets the documents are subsampled 8x for ICL. ICL is much stronger than FT on simple syllogisms. On a semantic-structure benchmark of 110 categories, ICL helps overall, most on reversals and syllogisms, but category holdout stays hard with minimal ICL gain. In our case FT generalizes more broadly, which suggests our asymmetry concerns behavioral defaults (a global answer format) rather than how content is used. Augmented FT suggests a bridge experiment: train on ICL-conditioned outputs.
verified.verification_note: The arXiv comments field says 'FoRLM workshop, NeurIPS 2025', so the venue was updated (workshop, not main track). I softened 'much stronger on the 110-category benchmark': the paper reports an overall benefit, with minimal gain on category holdout. verified.title: The Unlocking Spell on Base LLMs: Rethinking Alignment via In-Context Learning (URIAL)
verified.authors: Bill Yuchen Lin, Abhilasha Ravichander, Ximing Lu, Nouha Dziri, Melanie Sclar, Khyathi Chandu, Chandra Bhagavatula, Yejin Choi
verified.key_finding: On average 77.7% of the aligned model's tokens are also ranked top-1 by the base model (92.2% within the base model's top 3), and only about 5-8% are shifted. Shifted tokens are mostly stylistic ('However', 'Here', 'Thank', 'Hello', 'sorry'), and shifts are more pronounced at early positions. With K=3 restyled examples plus a system prompt, base models match or beat aligned models: Llama-2-70b URIAL 4.74 vs Llama-2-70b-chat 4.67, Mistral-7b URIAL 4.63 vs Mistral-7b-Instruct 4.44. For Llama-2-7b, K=8 (4.37) adds little over K=3 (4.33).
verified.relation: Explains our result. Style and format are the most superficial layer of alignment, and ICL can install them in base models with about 3 shots. Our null result comes from a chat model whose post-training already fixed a verbose style that shows its working, so ICL must override a strong prior rather than fill an empty one. Testable prediction: Qwen3-1.7B-Base should show a much larger ICL format effect.
verified.verification_note: All numbers confirmed in the arXiv HTML (Fig. 2/3 text and Table 1). The ICLR 2024 acceptance is confirmed by the ICLR virtual poster page and the OpenReview record.

verified.title: Is In-Context Learning Sufficient for Instruction Following in LLMs?
verified.authors: Hao Zhao, Maksym Andriushchenko, Francesco Croce, Nicolas Flammarion
verified.key_finding: URIAL trails instruction fine-tuning on MT-Bench: Llama-3-8B 5.75 vs 7.86, Llama-3-70B 6.40 vs 8.74. Many-shot ICL gains on the first turn plateau after 10-30 examples and turn slightly negative beyond 100 for Llama-3.1-8B. Second-turn scores keep decreasing as examples are added. In Appendix C, the in-context-aligned model's next-token distribution differs from the base model only for the first few tokens, after which KL rapidly drops to about 0. For IFT, KL does not converge to 0, and IFT on only 3 examples already moves the model far from the base. The authors conclude that 'ICL overfits to the style of the examples shown in context'.
verified.relation: Strongly supports and explains our result with the same asymmetry. A weight update shifts the output distribution globally and persistently, including outside the demonstrated setting (our GSM8K transfer). ICL's effect stays local to the demonstrated setting and to the first few tokens. The plateau suggests that going beyond 16 shots may not close the gap.
verified.verification_note: Numbers and quotes confirmed in v3 HTML. ICLR 2025 acceptance confirmed via the ICLR 2025 virtual poster page (iclr.cc/virtual/2025/poster/29602).

verified.title: Many-Shot In-Context Learning
verified.authors: Rishabh Agarwal, Avi Singh, Lei M. Zhang, Bernd Bohnet, Luis Rosias, Stephanie Chan, Biao Zhang, Ankesh Anand, Zaheer Abbas, Azade Nova, John D. Co-Reyes, Eric Chu, Feryal Behbahani, Aleksandra Faust, Hugo Larochelle
verified.key_finding: On Gemini 1.5 Pro, going from few-shot to hundreds or thousands of shots gives large gains, and 'many-shot ICL is effective at overriding pretraining biases'. On Financial PhraseBank, accuracy with flipped and abstract labels starts far below default labels and approaches them only with many shots. Because NLL gains need not show up in sampled behavior, the near-null ICL effect should also be measured in log-prob space. Caveat: frontier-scale model.
verified.verification_note: Findings confirmed in arXiv v3 HTML. The paper is slightly inconsistent on GPQA: §3.2 reports degradation at 250 shots and §4.8 a decline after 125. NeurIPS 2024 Spotlight confirmed via the NeurIPS proceedings page.

verified.title: Many-shot Jailbreaking
verified.authors: Cem Anil, Esin Durmus, Mrinank Sharma, Joe Benton, Sandipan Kundu, Joshua Batson, et al., Ethan Perez, Roger Grosse, David Duvenaud
verified.key_finding: Attack success follows −E[log P(harmful resp. | n shots)] = C·n^−α + K. On Claude 2.0 tasks the attack 'doesn't work at all with 5 shots' but 'works consistently with 256 shots'. On many tasks larger models learn faster in context (larger exponents), and safety-unrelated ICL tasks also follow power laws. Reformatting away from the user/assistant tags changes the intercept but not the slope. SL and RL alignment lower the zero-shot probability of harm (the NLL intercept rises) but leave the exponent largely unchanged. Demonstrations sampled narrowly from one category ('discrimination') fail to jailbreak a different target topic ('deception'); diverse demonstrations recover baseline. Fig. 6: after SL/RL on a benign answer distribution, the in-context slope on benign examples converges to 0.
verified.relation: Explains our result. At n=16, and for a small model with a presumably small α, little in-context movement is expected. Our advice-only demonstrations are narrow relative to the math target, which mirrors the narrow-topic transfer failure. Fine-tuning moves the intercept (the zero-shot default), and that intercept is what our GSM8K metric reads. Fig. 6 adds that once a distribution is trained in, further in-context examples of it add almost nothing. Caveat: the exponent-vs-size results are on Anthropic models, so extrapolating to Qwen3-1.7B is our inference.
verified.verification_note: Read the full PDF via pdftotext and confirmed the equation, the 5/256-shot sentence, the intercept-vs-slope statements and the narrow/diverse topic result. I corrected the wording 'lower the intercept' to 'reduce zero-shot harm probability (NLL intercept rises)' to match the paper. NeurIPS 2024 confirmed via the proceedings page.

verified.title: Bayesian scaling laws for in-context learning
verified.authors: Aryaman Arora, Dan Jurafsky, Christopher Potts, Noah D. Goodman
verified.key_finding: The paper models ICL as a Bayesian update with interpretable terms for task priors, an ICL efficiency coefficient and per-example probabilities. On GINC, probability is 'abruptly concentrated' on the SFT task once a threshold amount of SFT is passed, the threshold rises with model scale, and in-distribution scores change at about the same number of SFT examples for all sizes. Conclusion: 'smaller amounts of post-training strongly change the prior over tasks but not the model's knowledge of each task.' On Llama 3.1 8B, instruction tuning reduces the prior on unsafe behaviours but 'fails to prevent many-shot jailbreaking'.
verified.relation: Explains our result and gives a vocabulary for it. FT moves the prior over answer styles (a terse-verdict persona), and that global prior shows up on GSM8K. ICL only multiplies evidence by per-example likelihoods scaled by a model-specific efficiency, so 16 shots against a strong chat prior barely move the posterior. A prior shift is driven by the data, which may explain why the FT effect transfers to 14B (Spearman 0.63) while the ICL effect, which depends on model-specific efficiency, does not. The abrupt prior shift fits our fast saturation.
verified.verification_note: The arXiv abstract page comments read 'COLM 2025 camera-ready version'. I changed the venue from an unconfirmed arXiv preprint to COLM 2025 and the type to peer_reviewed. Findings confirmed in v4 HTML.

verified.title: Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs
verified.authors: Jan Betley, Daniel Tan, Niels Warncke, Anna Sztyber-Betley, Xuchan Bao, Martín Soto, Nathan Labenz, Owain Evans
verified.key_finding: GPT-4o fine-tuned on insecure code gives misaligned answers 20% of the time on selected unrelated questions (6% on pre-registered ones). In-context with k up to 256 insecure-code examples, GPT-4o gives 'no misaligned responses for any value of k', even though at k=128 and 256 it writes insecure code on held-out examples at a rate similar to the fine-tuned model. In Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, secure and insecure runs diverge 'around step 40' (the Discussion says about 50 steps). Follow-up Afonin et al. 2025 (arXiv 2510.11288) found ICL-induced EM with 16 narrow advice examples on some frontier models: Gemini 3 Pro 21.4% on narrow datasets and 24.2% on TruthfulQA. Qwen models were low: Qwen3-Next-80B-Instruct 0%/0%, Qwen3 Max 1.1%/1.3%, Qwen3-Next-80B-Thinking 0%/4.5%. 'Insecure code examples do not elicit misalignment from any tested model', which the authors attribute to a distribution mismatch between code examples and free-form questions.
verified.relation: A close parallel to our result. Narrow data delivered through the weights spills into broad out-of-domain behavior. The same data in context is imitated in-distribution but spills over little or not at all, at least for Qwen-family models (near 0%) and mismatched domains. GSM8K plays the role of their unrelated evaluation questions. The early divergence matches our fast onset. Afonin et al. show that in-context spillover is model-dependent and can happen in some frontier models, so our null may not be universal.
verified.verification_note: ICML 2025 confirmed via the PMLR v267 entry. I corrected the Qwen claim: not all Qwen models are at 0% in Afonin et al. (Qwen3 Max 1.1-1.3%, Qwen3-Next Thinking 4.5% on TruthfulQA). Afonin's '64 examples' for insecure code comes from a figure caption and is not clearly tied to that dataset alone. Step-40 vs ~50-step discrepancy noted.

verified.title: Language models transmit behavioural traits through hidden signals in data (arXiv title: Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data)
verified.authors: Alex Cloud, Minh Le, James Chua, Jan Betley, Anna Sztyber-Betley, Sören Mindermann, Jacob Hilton, Samuel Marks, Owain Evans
verified.key_finding: A student fine-tuned on number sequences from a teacher with a trait acquires that trait. When the same data is given in context to GPT-4.1 nano, with various numbers of examples and 'even when the entire dataset is included in context', 'ICL fails in every setting tested'. Theory: 'a single, sufficiently small step of gradient descent on any teacher-generated output necessarily moves the student toward the teacher, regardless of the training distribution', provided the student and teacher share the same initialization. Transmission fails across different base models (e.g. GPT-4.1 nano to Qwen2.5), except between GPT-4o and GPT-4.1.
verified.relation: Explains the mechanism. Gradient descent absorbs every statistical regularity in the targets, including ones the model would not recognize as task-relevant, and writes them into shared low-rank directions that act in every domain. ICL picks up only what the model reads as the task. The uniform terseness of the DSSE answers is that kind of global regularity: LoRA amplifies it everywhere, while the in-context reader treats it as local to advice. Caveat: the subliminal channel needs a shared initialization and our data was not generated by Qwen, so our effect is a non-hidden, overt format regularity rather than true subliminal transfer.
verified.verification_note: ICL result and theorem quotes confirmed in arXiv v1 HTML. Crossref shows the peer-reviewed version in Nature (15 Apr 2026, vol 652) under a changed title and with an added author (Sören Mindermann), so I updated the year, venue, authors and type. The Nature full text was paywalled and not read, so the ICL claim was verified only against the arXiv version.

open_questions: Base vs chat: is the ICL null tied to the chat model's post-trained style prior? URIAL installs style in base models with 3 shots, and Wei et al. 2023 (arXiv 2303.03846, abstract only) report that small and instruction-tuned models stick to their semantic priors. Run the same 16-shot context on Qwen3-1.7B-Base and on Qwen3-14B-chat (larger models have larger ICL power-law exponents in MSJ). Does the ICL format effect grow there, and does it start to correlate with the FT effect?

Dose-response: is n=16 just too low on the curve, or is it flat? For each dataset, fit −log p(commit-first or terse answer | n shots) = C·n^−α + K over n in {0,1,2,4,...,256}. Use teacher-forced log-probs, not sampled rates, because MSJ and Agarwal show log-prob catches small shifts and NLL can move without behavior. A small but real α would mean slow ICL. α ≈ 0 would mean the context route cannot reach the format at all.

Locality: do advice-only demonstrations fail only because ICL is topic-local? This is consistent with MSJ's narrow-topic failure, Afonin's code-vs-free-text mismatch and Zhao's finding that ICL overfits to the demonstrated style. Control: put terse no-working math answers, or mixed-domain terse answers, in context. If those remove the working on GSM8K, ICL can carry the format, and the asymmetry is about cross-domain generalization breadth rather than capability.

Prior vs efficiency: does FT mainly shift the intercept or prior, as SL/RL do in MSJ and SFT does in Arora et al., leaving ICL efficiency unchanged? Test by applying the 16-shot context on top of early checkpoints (e.g. step 8). If the effects add on a log-prob scale, the two routes act on the same quantity with very different strength. If they do not, they are separate mechanisms. A Bayesian-law fit could also test whether the prior-shift term, unlike K, is what transfers from 1.7B to 14B.

Token position: URIAL and Zhao et al. find that ICL shifts sit in the first few tokens, while IFT diverges throughout. Is our FT effect concentrated at the first answer token (a number vs 'Let's'/'To solve')? Compare per-position KL on GSM8K prompts for the FT and ICL conditions. If FT acts mainly at position 1, why ICL cannot flip that one early decision is the core question. Context distillation or Lampinen-style augmented FT on ICL-conditioned outputs could then tell whether the context signal is weak or just not consolidated.

verified.title: A General Language Assistant as a Laboratory for Alignment
verified.authors: Amanda Askell, Yuntao Bai, Anna Chen, Dawn Drain, Deep Ganguli, Tom Henighan, et al. (22 authors, Anthropic)
verified.key_finding: Section 2.1 introduces context distillation, L(θ)=D_KL(p0(X|C)||pθ(X)), where X comes from a large corpus. It argues that fine-tuning on C moves the data prior P(X) toward the prompt's distribution, while prompting gives P(X|C). Toy example (Fig. 26): models fine-tuned on 1,2,...,63 become confident at counting but never learn that 64, 65, ... should come next, whereas a prompted model expects them. Appendix B.5: the targets were the top-50 log-probs (a 51-way KL with an 'other' bucket) of the HHH-prompted 52B model, on a half-and-half mix of pretraining data and Stack Exchange formatted as Assistant answers. All model sizes were fine-tuned on these targets. 'For many but not all of our evaluations context distillation performs about as well as prompting.' Contractors rated it slightly worse than the full prompt.
verified.relation: Explains the result. Hard-target SFT on 150 terse rows changes the unconditional prior over assistant turns, so the terse format can reach GSM8K. The 16 in-context turns instead give P(X|C). Design: context-distill the 16-shot teacher into the same LoRA (KL on teacher log-probs over a mix of advice and GSM8K prompts). If the student keeps the ICL profile (math wrong about 0.27), the format comes from the hard-target objective, not from the weight route as such.
verified.verification_note: Read the full PDF text with pdftotext. The equation, the Sec. 2.1 argument, the counting toy and the B.5 details are all confirmed. One correction: the original said 'for the 52B model the targets were...'. In fact the 52B prompted model produced the targets and all model sizes were distilled on them. The abstract does not mention context distillation, but the body does (Sec. 2.1, App. B.5).

verified.title: Learning by Distilling Context
verified.authors: Charlie Snell, Dan Klein, Ruiqi Zhong
verified.key_finding: The teacher sees [instructions/examples]+[task input], and the same model is trained to reproduce the teacher's answer from the task input alone. The loss is a token-level KL, with soft labels approximated by 100 sampled tokens; the authors reject hard-label SFT on the sampled answer as wasteful and noisy. On SPIDER with Incoder-6.7B (exact-set match, Table 2), with 4 examples: teacher 27.7, student before distillation 0.3, after distillation 22.1, direct gradient descent on the same examples 13.4. With 8 examples: 28.2 / 0.3 / 27.9 / 18.9. Distillation beats direct GD by 8.6 points (4-shot) and 9.0 points (8-shot), and the distilled student approaches the teacher with context.
verified.relation: Shows that putting the same examples into the weights by context distillation gives different behavior from hard-label gradient descent, and that the distilled student tracks the context-conditioned teacher. Prediction for us: a student distilled from the 16-shot-context Qwen3-1.7B should inherit the small ICL-sized GSM8K effect. Our hypothesis (not the paper's claim) is that hard-label SFT is a different operator that can install a format the teacher never showed. Caveat: distillation also trains on many synthetic unlabeled task inputs, so the comparison mixes objective with input coverage. A clean control should match inputs.
verified.verification_note: Read the full PDF text. All Table 2 numbers match exactly. I found no peer-reviewed venue (no OpenReview or proceedings entry), so it stays a preprint. Added the 100-sample soft-label detail and the caveat that the student sees synthetic inputs.

verified.title: Prefix-Tuning: Optimizing Continuous Prompts for Generation
verified.authors: Xiang Lisa Li, Percy Liang
verified.key_finding: Prefix-tuning trains about 0.1% of parameters (per-layer continuous prefix activations, with GPT-2 or BART frozen). It is comparable to fine-tuning on table-to-text with full data and slightly below fine-tuning on XSUM summarization. In low-data settings (50-500 examples, averaged over 10 models per size) it beats fine-tuning by 2.9 BLEU on average, and the gap narrows as data grows. It extrapolates better to unseen topics (XSUM news-to-sports R-L 31.51 vs 30.26; WebNLG unseen categories). Initializing the prefix with activations of real words clearly beats random initialization in low-data settings; random initialization gives low performance with high variance.
verified.relation: Our 150-row setting falls in their low-data regime, and a prefix is the natural intermediate object between the 16-shot context and a LoRA. Design: initialize a prefix from the KV activations of the 16 in-context rows, train it with the same SFT loss and step budget as the LoRA, and track GSM8K working and wrong rates per step. That shows whether, and when, a cache-resident object acquires the format. Caveat: their better extrapolation is desired task transfer, so a prefix could also carry the format to math. This has to be tested, not assumed.
verified.verification_note: Read the full PDF text. 2.9 BLEU, 31.51 vs 30.26 and the initialization result are all confirmed. Corrected 'matches fine-tuning with full data': this holds for table-to-text, while Table 2 shows prefix-tuning slightly underperforms on XSUM. The venue is confirmed as ACL Anthology 2021.acl-long.353 (pp. 4582-4597).

verified.title: The Power of Scale for Parameter-Efficient Prompt Tuning
verified.authors: Brian Lester, Rami Al-Rfou, Noah Constant
verified.key_finding: With T5, soft prompts on a frozen model match full model tuning only at the largest scale (XXL, 11B). Prompt tuning is more robust to domain shift. Trained on SQuAD, it beats model tuning on 4 of 6 MRQA out-of-domain sets, most on TextbookQA (+12.5 F1, 66.8 vs 54.3), and is worse on DuoRC (-1.2) and DROP (-1.8). On QQP->MRPC it is better by +3.2 accuracy and +3.1 F1; the reverse direction is close to a tie. The authors argue that freezing the model 'prevents the model from modifying its general understanding of language'. Prompts 'indirectly modulate the representation of the input', whereas adapters modify the function by 'allowing the rewriting of activations at any given layer'.
verified.relation: Predicts that a soft prompt trained on the terse advice rows would cause less off-domain behavior change (GSM8K format) than a LoRA. This matches the hypothesis that a prompt or cache holds the format more locally. At 1.7B, prompt tuning may underfit the in-domain target, so in-domain brevity (about 28 words) must be matched before comparing GSM8K side effects. Otherwise a null result just reflects weaker learning; their own robustness results are at T5-XXL scale.
verified.verification_note: Read the full PDF text. The arXiv comments field says 'Accepted to EMNLP 2021'. The quotes and numbers are confirmed. Added that prompt tuning wins on 4 of 6 OOD sets, not all of them, and that the comparison is at XXL scale.

verified.title: When Do Prompting and Prefix-Tuning Work? A Theory of Capabilities and Limitations
verified.authors: Aleksandar Petrov, Philip H.S. Torr, Adel Bibi
verified.key_finding: Prompting, ICL, soft prompting and prefix-tuning cannot change the relative attention pattern over content tokens. They can only scale it down and add a bias to each attention block's output. That bias lies in a subspace of rank at most the prefix length n_S, which in practice is not fully used, and it is scaled by how much each position attends to the prefix. Full fine-tuning (ΔWQ, ΔWK, ΔWV) allows content-dependent changes. So context methods can elicit or combine pretrained skills but may not learn tasks that need new attention patterns. In a toy test, a 1-layer transformer pretrained to sort ascending can be fully fine-tuned to sort descending, but prefix-tuning cannot do it.
verified.relation: Gives a mechanistic reason the context route stays local. A terse verdict is a pretrained skill, so a prefix can express it, but the bias strength depends on attention to the prefix and is therefore gated by content. A GSM8K query that attends little to advice-shaped context gets little bias, while a LoRA delta applies to every token. Testable: compare attention mass on the 16 context turns (and on a trained prefix) for advice versus GSM8K queries, and check whether it predicts per-dataset in-context effect sizes.
verified.verification_note: Read the full PDF text. arXiv says 'Accepted at ICLR 2024'; it was first posted in Oct 2023. The claims are confirmed. Added the paper's own remark that prefixes do not span the full rank-n_S subspace in practice. The sorting experiments use small toy transformers.

verified.title: Cartridges: Lightweight and general-purpose long context representations via self-study
verified.authors: Sabri Eyuboglu, Ryan Ehrlich, Simran Arora, Neel Guha, Dylan Zinsley, Emily Liu, Will Tennien, Atri Rudra, James Zou, Azalia Mirhoseini, Christopher Re
verified.venue: arXiv preprint 2506.06266 (also ES-FoMo III workshop at ICML 2025, oral)
verified.key_finding: A trained KV cache (a 'Cartridge') is learned offline per corpus. Naive next-token training on the corpus memorizes it but is not competitive with ICL. Self-study (synthetic conversations about the corpus plus KL to the model with the subcorpus in context, Eq. 3) matches ICL at 38.6x less memory and 26.4x higher throughput. On the same synthetic data, the context-distillation objective beats next-token prediction by 8.6 chrF on MTOB (24.9 -> 33.5). In the parameterization ablation, LoRA cartridges drop MMLU from 54.7 to 45.3 as size grows from 0.15 to 1.06 GB. Prefix/KV cartridges drop only from 54.7 to 54.3. Prefix is also +4.5 chrF better in-domain at about 0.6 GB on MTOB. Initializing from KV vectors of the first p corpus tokens beats random-token KV and random vectors (LongHealth 55.3 vs 51.3 vs 29.9). Independently trained cartridges can be composed without retraining.
verified.relation: The closest direct evidence that one objective in a KV-cache parameterization does far less off-target damage than in LoRA. This is our question with MMLU in place of GSM8K format. It sets up the core 2x2: {LoRA, KV cartridge initialized from the 16-shot cache} x {hard-target SFT on 150 rows, KL distillation from the 16-shot teacher}. Measure GSM8K working rate and 14B transfer per dataset. If the hard-target cartridge installs the format, the format can live in a cache and the ICL null is about the objective. If only hard-target LoRA does, parameterization matters. Note that their LoRA-vs-prefix ablation uses the distillation objective and very large LoRA ranks (up to 1632).
verified.verification_note: Read the full PDF text (v3). Corrected '24.9 -> 33.5 over naive': this number compares the context-distillation and next-token objectives on the same self-study synthetic data, not self-study versus naive corpus training. The paper is internally inconsistent: the main text says MMLU fell 54.7 -> 45.3 for LoRA, while Appendix A.1 says 60.0 -> 45.3 at 1.06 GB (LoRA rank 1632). The ICML 2025 ES-FoMo workshop oral is listed on the Stanford project page; there is no main-conference proceedings entry.

verified.title: Inoculation Prompting: Eliciting traits from LLMs during training can suppress them at test-time
verified.authors: Daniel Tan, Anders Woodruff, Niels Warncke, Arun Jose, Maxime Riché, David Demitri Africa, Mia Taylor
verified.venue: ICLR 2026 (poster; listed there as '...can reduce trait expression at test-time'; arXiv 2510.04340, 2025)
verified.key_finding: During fine-tuning, the method prepends a system prompt that deliberately elicits the unwanted trait; evaluation is done without it. Inoculated models express the trait much less at test time. Tested on GPT-4.1 (with a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct replication, plus GPT-4.1-mini and Qwen2.5-32B for EM) across toy trait pairs, emergent misalignment, backdoors and subliminal learning. The effect is selective: with Spanish+ALL-CAPS data, 'You always speak in Spanish' yields English, often capitalized responses. In GPT-4.1, Spanish-inoculation also partly impairs capitalization learning; the Qwen results are cleaner. In the EM setting, semantically irrelevant (Trigger) and Placebo prompts do not inoculate. Proposed mechanism: making a trait less surprising 'reduces optimization pressure to globally update the model'. Wichers et al. 2025 (arXiv 2510.05024) independently find that prompts which more strongly elicit the behavior before fine-tuning inoculate better.
verified.relation: Frames the context route as 'context explains the data'. Training data that the context already accounts for creates little pressure for a global weight change. Our 16-shot context explains the targets only weakly (advice 396 -> 215 words, not 28), which may be why it also induces little. Design: fine-tune with an explicit format instruction ('answer in 1-2 sentences, no working') or the 16-shot context in the prompt, evaluate without it, and predict restored GSM8K working. Also compute the per-dataset target log-prob gain from context and test whether this 'surprise reduction' predicts the FT effect, the effect that ICL size itself fails to predict (Spearman -0.08).
verified.verification_note: Read the full PDF text (v4). The ICLR 2026 acceptance is confirmed via the iclr.cc virtual poster page, which uses the slightly different title. Updated the type to peer_reviewed and the year to 2026. Added the GPT-4.1 caveat on selectivity and that the Placebo/Trigger result comes from the EM setting. I also read the Wichers et al. abstract and confirmed its claim.

verified.title: Emergent Misalignment is Easy, Narrow Misalignment is Hard
verified.authors: Anna Soligo, Edward Turner, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Neel Nanda
verified.key_finding: On Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, a single residual steering vector trained at layer 24 on bad-medical-advice data yields 28% general (out-of-domain) misalignment, comparable to rank-1 or rank-32 adapters at the same layer, and 52% narrow misalignment. Mixing in aligned data from other domains fails to confine learning: it lowers general and narrow misalignment together. A narrow solution appears only with a KL penalty to the chat model on other-domain advice data (λ=1e6 for steering vectors, 1e5 for LoRA). The general solution reaches lower training loss at smaller parameter norm and degrades less under orthogonal noise. When the KL term is removed and training continues, the narrow solution converges back to the general one.
verified.relation: A steering vector is a constant, always-on residual bias. In our reading (not the paper's claim) it is functionally like an ungated prefix, and it still generalizes broadly. So the key variable is probably whether the bias is gated by context, not weights versus context. The paper also suggests that 'terse everywhere' is the efficient general solution SFT finds early, which fits half the effect after 8 of 76 steps. Direct test: add a KL penalty on GSM8K-style prompts during SFT. If advice brevity survives while math working returns, the format is a removable general solution rather than something the data requires. Per their mixing result, simply adding worked math examples to the training data may not be enough.
verified.verification_note: Read the full PDF text. The header says 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026', and the iclr.cc poster page confirms it. The 28%, the layer-24 placement and the λ values (Table 9) are confirmed. The model is identified as Qwen-14B / Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct in the appendix tables and figures; Sec. 3 does not name it explicitly. Added the 52% narrow figure and the finding that mixing in aligned data does not confine learning.

verified.title: Self-Distillation Bridges Distribution Gap in Language Model Fine-Tuning
verified.authors: Zhaorui Yang, Tianyu Pang, Haozhe Feng, Han Wang, Wei Chen, Minfeng Zhu, Qian Liu
verified.key_finding: Setup: Llama-2-7b-chat with LoRA r=8. Vanilla SFT on OpenFunctions drops off-target GSM8K from 29.4 to 21.5 and HumanEval pass@1 from 13.4 to 9.8. SDFT keeps GSM8K at 29.1 and raises HumanEval to 15.2, with comparable or better target-task performance. SDFT fine-tunes on the seed model's own rewrites of the dataset responses. After GSM8K fine-tuning, the AlpacaEval win rate falls from 66.04 to 23.38 with vanilla SFT and is 66.73 with SDFT. The authors name the distribution gap between task-dataset targets and the seed LM's own distribution as the main cause of forgetting.
verified.relation: Supports a target-distribution explanation for why the weight route installs format. Our targets are far off the model's own distribution (28 vs 396 words), and hard-label SFT has to pull the global prior toward them; the ICL route never imposes this gap. Design: rewrite the 150 rows in Qwen3-1.7B's own style while keeping each verdict (SDFT-style) and check whether the GSM8K format effect disappears. Also test per-dataset target NLL under the base model as a predictor of FT effect size and of 14B transfer.
verified.verification_note: Read the full PDF text. All numbers and r=8 are confirmed. ACL Anthology lists it as 2024.acl-long.58 (pp. 1028-1043). Minor detail: the text gives the seed AlpacaEval score as 66.03, while the table gives 66.04.

open_questions: Route or objective? Run the 2x2 {LoRA, trained KV-cache/prefix initialized from the 16-shot cache} x {hard-target SFT on the 150 rows, KL distillation from the 16-shot-context teacher}, matching in-domain advice length (about 28 words) where possible. The question is whether the GSM8K format effect (working 1.00 -> 0.62) follows the parameterization, the loss, or both. Snell/Askell predict that distilled students inherit the ICL near-null. Cartridges/Lester predict smaller side effects for cache parameterizations even under hard targets.

Is the context route gated by attention? Petrov et al. imply that a prefix's influence on a GSM8K query scales with how much that query attends to the advice context. Does attention mass on the 16 in-context turns (or a trained prefix) collapse on math queries compared with advice queries? Does per-dataset attention mass explain the in-context effect sizes that are uncorrelated with the FT effect (Spearman -0.08)?

Does the 16-shot context 'explain away' the targets? Measure per dataset how much the context raises the log-probability of the terse targets (the 'surprise reduction' in inoculation prompting). Does this, rather than ICL behavioral change, predict FT effect size and 14B transfer? And does fine-tuning with the context or an explicit brevity instruction in the prompt (then removed at test time) inoculate against the GSM8K format effect?

Is 'terse everywhere' the cheap general solution? Following Soligo et al., add a KL penalty on GSM8K-style prompts during SFT and compare loss and update norm of the narrow versus general solutions. Does the general solution's efficiency explain why half the effect appears after only 8 of 76 steps? Does a plain steering vector trained on the rows (ungated, always-on) reproduce the LoRA's format transfer even though it is 'context-like'?

Why does ICL transmit broad emergent misalignment in some models (Afonin et al. 2025 report 1-24% EM with 16 narrow in-context examples) but not a response format here? Is format interpreted per-query (the model re-infers the task from a math question) while persona/values are inferred per-conversation? Would a many-shot context (64-256 rows) or a system-prompt framing that presents the rows as the assistant's own style close the gap?
